questions.stem: Use the glucose log to fill in the diagram: the problem this client most likely has, 2 actions for the nurse, and 2 parameters to track.

condition.text: Nocturnal hypoglycemia with morning rebound (Somogyi effect)

actions.text: Ask for the evening NPH dose to be reduced
Increase the evening NPH dose as the client asked
Move all of the insulin doses to the morning
Stop checking the glucose during the night

rationale.correct: A 0300 low with a high fasting glucose after more evening insulin is the Somogyi effect: reduce the evening dose, not increase it.

perOption.c1: A 0300 low followed by a high fasting glucose after an evening NPH increase.
perOption.c2: In dawn phenomenon, the 0300 glucose is normal or high.
perOption.a1: Less overnight insulin stops the low and the rebound.
perOption.a5: The 0300 check is how the problem was found.
perOption.p1: Confirms the pattern and the fix.
perOption.p2: Should fall as the rebound stops.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish the Somogyi effect from the dawn phenomenon.

questions.stem: A client with DKA is on an insulin infusion. For each finding at hour 14, choose how the nurse should interpret it.

cells.text: Stop the infusion now and give basal insulin at 2100

options.text: Closed: the ketoacidosis has resolved
Still open
Not useful for DKA
On target while insulin continues
Too high; increase the insulin
Hypoglycemia
Ready to change to subcutaneous insulin
Not ready
Needs to stay NPO
Unsafe: give basal insulin 1 to 2 hours before stopping the infusion
Safe
Unnecessary to give basal insulin

rationale.correct: When the gap closes and the client eats, give basal insulin 1 to 2 hours before stopping the infusion.

perOption.b1:a: A gap of 12 or less with bicarbonate of 18 or more marks resolution.
perOption.b1:b: It is in the normal range.
perOption.b2:a: Dextrose keeps glucose up so insulin can clear ketones.
perOption.b2:b: The target is about 150 to 200 during treatment.
perOption.b3:a: Gap closed and eating are the criteria.
perOption.b4:a: IV insulin lasts minutes; without overlap, ketosis returns.
perOption.b4:b: There would be hours with no insulin.

references: American Diabetes Association Standards of Care
Written as part of a full NGN case study to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.stem: On an endocrine unit, the nurse has four new findings at the same time. Which client should the nurse go to first?

options.text: A client with Addison disease whose morning hydrocortisone is 30 minutes late and who feels tired
A client 6 hours after thyroidectomy who says their lips feel numb and tingly
A client on an insulin infusion whose glucose is 62 mg/dL and who is sweating and confused
A client with diabetes insipidus who has finished a jug of water and is asking for another

rationale.correct: Symptomatic hypoglycemia on an insulin infusion is the most immediate threat.

perOption.a: Give the dose soon, but the client is stable.
perOption.b: Early hypocalcemia needs assessment soon; the airway is not yet threatened.
perOption.c: Symptomatic hypoglycemia on IV insulin can deteriorate within minutes.
perOption.d: Thirst is protective; replace the water and continue monitoring.

questions.stem: Which tasks can the RN delegate to the unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP) on an endocrine unit? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check and record a fingerstick glucose on a stable client
Measure and record urine output every hour for a client with DI
Report a glucose below 70 mg/dL to the RN at once
Decide whether a client with a glucose of 62 mg/dL needs juice or IV dextrose
Adjust an insulin infusion rate
Teach a client how to use an insulin pen

rationale.correct: UAPs can measure, record and report; decisions, medication changes and teaching stay with the RN.

perOption.e: Medication titration is the RN's role.

rows.text: Blood pressure 238/130 mm Hg
Heart rate 138/min with palpitations
Pale skin
Glucose 212 mg/dL
Sweating

questions.stem: Complete the sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

content.template: The client is in {{b1}}. Giving a beta blocker before an alpha blocker would {{b2}} because {{b3}}.

options.text: a catecholamine hypertensive crisis
a panic attack
thyroid storm
hypoglycemia
raise the blood pressure further
safely lower the blood pressure
cure the tumor
have no effect
blocking beta-2 vasodilation leaves alpha vasoconstriction unopposed
beta blockers raise heart rate
beta blockers release catecholamines
the tumor is on the left

rationale.correct: Alpha blockade always comes before beta blockade in pheochromocytoma.

perOption.b1:a: Risks stroke, MI and heart failure.
perOption.b1:b: The labs and mass show a tumor.

Phenoxybenzamine for 10 to 14 days before surgery
A high-salt diet and fluids once alpha-blocked
Metoprolol now for the heart rate
Deep palpation of the abdomen to feel the mass
Metoclopramide for nausea

perOption.r3:c2: Restores the contracted blood volume and prevents hypotension.

questions.stem: The client had a left adrenalectomy. Review the findings 3 hours after surgery. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Treat the glucose of 52 mg/dL per protocol
Give the prescribed fluid bolus for the low blood pressure
Check glucose every hour for the next 24 hours
Notify the surgeon of the blood pressure and glucose
Restart phenoxybenzamine to prevent a crisis
Raise the head of the bed to 90 degrees

rationale.correct: After adrenalectomy for pheochromocytoma, hypotension and rebound hypoglycemia are common.

perOption.a: Insulin rebounds when catecholamines fall suddenly.
perOption.b: Vessels dilate after the catecholamine source is gone.
perOption.e: The tumor is gone; this would worsen hypotension.

Stay upright for at least 30 minutes after taking it
Wait 30 minutes before eating, drinking or other medicines
Take it with orange juice or coffee
Take calcium at the same time

questions.stem: The correction insulin order is: 1 unit of insulin lispro for every 30 mg/dL above 150 mg/dL, rounded down to the nearest whole unit, added to the mealtime dose. The client's prelunch glucose is 312 mg/dL. How many units of correction insulin should the nurse give? Record your answer as a whole number.

rationale.correct: 312 - 150 = 162. 162 / 30 = 5.4, rounded down to 5 units, given with the mealtime dose.

questions.stem: For each statement, indicate whether it is accurate or inaccurate.

testSets.title: NCLEX-RN adaptive exam
testSets.description: Works like the real NCLEX-RN: each question depends on your answers so far, and the exam stops once your result is clear, after 85 to 150 questions. Choose timed (5 hours) or untimed. No going back; answers and rationales at the end. The questions are being rewritten to real NCLEX difficulty and recalibrated, so treat your result as a practice estimate.
